findings.title: Failed work is marked complete and can be committed
findings.body: The `finally` block marks every work item complete, including items whose `result_processor` raised an exception. The commit loop can then advance past a message whose processing failed, permanently losing its result. Only mark the offset complete after successful processing, or preserve the failure so it can be retried.

findings.title: Offset gaps can permanently block commits
findings.body: This tracker requires every integer offset between the last committed offset and the next completed message to appear in `all_offsets`. Kafka can legitimately deliver messages with gaps in offsets, for example because of compaction or aborted transactions; those missing offsets will never be submitted, so commits stop advancing and tracked offsets accumulate indefinitely. Track the order of delivered messages rather than requiring contiguous integer offsets.

findings.title: The work queues are unbounded
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` defaults to unlimited capacity, so a sustained input rate above worker throughput keeps accumulating work in memory instead of applying backpressure. Under overload this can grow until the consumer process runs out of memory; use bounded queues and handle the resulting backpressure.

findings.title: Shutdown exits workers without draining queued work
findings.body: Setting `worker.shutdown` makes the loop exit after the current item, even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to let the queue drain. Any remaining queued messages are abandoned without being processed or committed, so shutdown causes those messages to be replayed and may duplicate side effects. Drain queued items before exiting, or explicitly account for them during shutdown.
